mcqs.q: Dental plaque is best described as a:
opts: Structured, resilient biofilm of more than 500 microbial species
mcqs.explain: Plaque is a structured, resilient yellow-grayish biofilm adhering to intra-oral hard surfaces, containing more than 500 distinct microbial species.

mcqs.q: Dental plaque is classified by its position relative to the gingival margin as:
mcqs.explain: Plaque is classified as supragingival and subgingival based on its position from the gingival margin.

mcqs.q: Bacteria that are NOT within the biofilm but float freely are termed:
mcqs.explain: Bacteria may exist within the plaque biofilm or be free-floating (planktonic).

mcqs.q: Marginal plaque is most associated with the initiation of:
mcqs.explain: Marginal plaque is associated with the initiation and development of gingivitis; tissue-associated subgingival plaque causes periodontitis destruction.

mcqs.q: Tissue-associated subgingival plaque is linked to:
mcqs.explain: Tissue-associated subgingival plaque causes the tissue destruction seen in periodontitis.

mcqs.q: Bacteria associated with periodontal HEALTH are predominantly:
mcqs.explain: Periodontal health is dominated by gram-positive facultative species, with small proportions of gram-negatives and few spirochetes/motile rods.

mcqs.q: Which is a beneficial/protective species that resists pathogen colonization?
mcqs.explain: Beneficial species such as Streptococcus sanguinis prevent the colonization or proliferation of pathogenic micro-organisms.

mcqs.q: Active periodontal destruction requires a susceptible host, pathogenic species and:
opts: Absence or small proportion of beneficial bacteria
mcqs.explain: Destruction requires a susceptible host, pathogenic species and the absence/small proportion of beneficial bacteria.

mcqs.q: The microbial imbalance that drives periodontal destruction is called:
mcqs.explain: Dysbiosis (loss of microbial balance) leads to periodontal destruction; small amounts of balanced plaque are controlled by host defences.

mcqs.q: Pregnancy-associated gingivitis is particularly associated with:
mcqs.explain: Pregnancy-associated gingivitis is associated with Prevotella intermedia and Campylobacter rectus.

mcqs.q: Periodontitis is associated with which group of bacteria?
opts: Anaerobic gram-negative — P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, F. nucleatum
mcqs.explain: Periodontitis shows elevated spirochetes and anaerobic (90%) gram-negative (75%) species — Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Prevotella intermedia, Fusobacterium nucleatum, etc.

mcqs.q: Molar-incisor pattern periodontitis is dominated (~90%) by:
mcqs.explain: In molar-incisor pattern periodontitis, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans (a capnophilic anaerobic rod) comprises ~90% of the microbiota.

mcqs.q: Necrotizing periodontal disease is characterised by:
opts: Necrosis of the marginal gingiva & interdental papillae, with pain & malodor
mcqs.explain: Necrotizing periodontal disease is acute inflammation with necrosis of marginal gingiva and interdental papillae, associated with stress or HIV, pain, malodor and possibly systemic symptoms.

mcqs.q: Necrotizing periodontal disease is associated with which predisposing factors?
mcqs.explain: Necrotizing periodontal disease is associated with stress or HIV infection (immunosuppression); spirochetes and F. nucleatum are present.

mcqs.q: Peri-implantitis is:
opts: An inflammatory process around an osseointegrated implant causing loss of supporting bone
mcqs.explain: Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory process around an osseointegrated implant that results in loss of supporting bone (A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis, T. forsythia).

mcqs.q: Periodontal disease results from:
opts: A complex interplay between the subgingival biofilm and the host immune–inflammatory response
Host response alone with no bacteria
mcqs.explain: Periodontal disease results from a complex interplay between the subgingival biofilm and the host immune–inflammatory events in the periodontal tissues.

mcqs.q: A key (paradoxical) concept of periodontal pathogenesis is that:
opts: The protective host inflammatory response causes most of the tissue damage
Bacteria directly destroy all the bone
mcqs.explain: The defensive processes, protective by intent, result in the majority of the tissue damage that produces the clinical disease.

mcqs.q: The MAIN determinant of susceptibility to periodontitis is:
opts: The nature of the host immune–inflammatory response
mcqs.explain: The main determinant of susceptibility to disease is the nature of the immune–inflammatory responses themselves.

mcqs.q: In clinically HEALTHY gingiva, which cell maintains a low-grade response to crevicular bacteria?
mcqs.explain: Healthy gingival connective tissue contains neutrophils (plus lymphocytes & macrophages) giving a low-grade, steady-state response to the bacterial biofilm.

mcqs.q: Regarding the gingivitis–periodontitis relationship:
opts: Gingivitis precedes periodontitis, but not all gingivitis progresses to periodontitis
mcqs.explain: Gingivitis precedes periodontitis, but not all gingivitis progresses to periodontitis.

mcqs.q: Gingivitis differs from periodontitis in that the inflammatory lesion is:
opts: Confined to the gingiva (no attachment/bone loss)
mcqs.explain: In gingivitis the lesion is confined to the gingiva; in periodontitis it extends to the PDL and alveolar bone, causing attachment and bone loss.

mcqs.q: Gingivitis is considered:
opts: Reversible if the bacterial challenge is reduced
mcqs.explain: Gingivitis is reversible if the bacterial challenge is reduced.

mcqs.q: The INITIAL (Stage I) gingival lesion (2–4 days) is dominated by which cell?
mcqs.explain: The initial lesion (2–4 days) shows vascular dilation and PMN (neutrophil) infiltration; it is subclinical with increased gingival fluid flow.

mcqs.q: The EARLY (Stage II) gingival lesion (4–7 days) shows an increase in which cell, with bleeding on probing?
mcqs.explain: The early lesion (4–7 days) shows increased T lymphocytes, rete-peg formation and collagen loss, with erythema and bleeding on probing.

mcqs.q: The ESTABLISHED (Stage III) gingival lesion (14–21 days) is dominated by:
mcqs.explain: The established lesion (14–21 days) is dominated by plasma cells, with changes in gingival size, colour and texture.

mcqs.q: The ADVANCED (Stage IV) lesion is significant because destructive changes:
opts: Extend into bone, causing attachment and bone loss (periodontitis)
mcqs.explain: In the advanced lesion, destructive changes extend into bone and other periodontal tissues, causing attachment loss and bone loss — i.e. periodontitis.

mcqs.q: In periodontitis, which cell dominates the connective tissue?
mcqs.explain: In periodontitis, plasma cells dominate in the connective tissues as collagen destruction extends into the PDL and bone.

mcqs.q: A periodontal pocket forms when the:
opts: Junctional epithelium migrates apically along the root surface
mcqs.explain: The junctional epithelium migrates apically along the root surface to maintain an intact epithelial barrier, forming a periodontal pocket.

mcqs.q: During alveolar bone resorption, which cells increase to destroy bone?
mcqs.explain: As inflammation reaches the marrow spaces, multinuclear osteoclasts and mononuclear phagocytes increase, thinning trabeculae and reducing bone height.

mcqs.q: Bone 'retreats' from the advancing inflammatory front mainly to:
opts: Defend against the spread of bacteria into the bone
mcqs.explain: Bone retreats from the advancing inflammatory front as a defence mechanism to prevent the spread of bacteria into the bone, resulting in bone loss.

mcqs.q: Individual susceptibility to periodontal disease is:
opts: Genetically determined and influenced by environmental risk factors (e.g. smoking)
mcqs.explain: Susceptibility is genetically determined and influenced by environmental risk factors such as smoking.

mcqs.q: The predominant gram-POSITIVE genera in subgingival plaque are:
mcqs.explain: The predominant gram-positive species in subgingival microbiota are Streptococcus and Actinomyces.

saqs.q: Define dental plaque and state how it is classified.
saqs.a: Dental plaque is a structured, resilient biofilm that adheres tenaciously to intra-oral hard surfaces and contains more than 500 microbial species. It is classified by position into supragingival and subgingival plaque.

saqs.q: Describe the site specificity of plaque in periodontal disease.
saqs.a: Marginal plaque → initiation of gingivitis; supragingival & tooth-associated subgingival → calculus and root caries; tissue-associated subgingival → tissue destruction in periodontitis.

saqs.q: Contrast the bacteria of periodontal health and periodontitis.
saqs.a: Health: mainly gram-positive facultative species (e.g. beneficial Streptococcus sanguinis). Periodontitis: anaerobic gram-negative species — Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Prevotella intermedia, Fusobacterium nucleatum, with elevated spirochetes (and A. actinomycetemcomitans in molar-incisor pattern).

saqs.q: What is dysbiosis, and what three conditions allow active periodontal destruction?
saqs.a: Dysbiosis = a microbial imbalance that drives periodontal destruction. Active destruction needs: 1) a susceptible host, 2) pathogenic species, and 3) the absence/small proportion of beneficial bacteria.

saqs.q: List the four stages of gingivitis with their predominant cells.
saqs.a: Initial (2–4 d, PMNs), Early (4–7 d, lymphocytes), Established (14–21 d, plasma cells), Advanced (bone involvement, plasma cells → periodontitis).

saqs.q: How does a periodontal pocket form?
saqs.a: Plasma-cell-dominated inflammation destroys collagen into the PDL/bone; the junctional epithelium migrates apically along the root to maintain the barrier, forming a periodontal pocket. As it deepens, bacteria proliferate apically and escape the inflammatory response.

saqs.q: Describe the pathogenesis of alveolar bone resorption.
saqs.a: Inflammation reaches the bone and spreads into the marrow spaces; multinuclear osteoclasts and mononuclear phagocytes increase, causing thinning of trabeculae, enlarged marrow spaces and reduced bone height. Bone retreats from the advancing front as a defence.
